name: Roman Empire (Theodosius I)

territory.border: hb:400:Western Roman Empire + hb:400:Eastern Roman Empire

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 4.0-4.5 million km2 for 285-394 CE (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/71). Border: the world_400 Western Roman Empire (2,361,040 km2) and Eastern Roman Empire (1,829,503 km2) polygons (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps/master/geojson/world_400.geojson, computed on the sphere) total 4.19 million km2 (mid); northern Britain beyond York is outside them. audit 2026-10-30: border changed from the four world_300 tetrarchy polygons (95 years off, 4.30M km2) to world_400 (5 years off); mid follows the new polygon.

population.note: Seshat codes the Dominate at 40-70 million for 300 CE; the high end is trimmed because the Antonine and Cyprian plagues and the 3rd-century crisis left the late-4th-century empire below its 2nd-century peak (rome-117 snapshot: ~56 million). Seshat codes the Eastern empire alone at 15 million for 400 CE (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/72), which implies a West of 25-35 million for the mid. Everything inside the border, slaves included; federate Goths settled in Thrace and Moesia in 382 are included.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Below the 2nd-century 20-25% of Hanson & Ortman 2017 (doi:10.1017/S1047759400074134): western cities had shrunk behind 3rd-century walls, while eastern cities (Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople at ~300,000 per Seshat https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/72) still flourished.

activePersonnel.note: Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964), vol. 2 ch. XVII "Numbers", pp. 679-684 (https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02): applying unit establishments to the Notitia Dignitatum gives East field armies 104,000, Eastern limitanei ~250,000, scholae 3,500 (East total ~357,500), Western field armies 113,000 and limitanei 135,500 c. 425, which Jones raises for the late 4th century (Rhine garrison comparable with the Upper Danube 81,000 or Lower Danube 64,000; Africa ~30,000). Empire-wide paper total ~600,000, "roughly consonant" with Agathias' figure of 645,000 for the old army (ancient, high). Jones stresses this is a paper strength well above effectives (dead men, deserters, fictitious soldiers on the rolls), and the Eastern field army had lost heavily at Adrianople (378) and both halves at the Frigidus (394), so mid ~505,000 and low 400,000 (cf. Strobel's ~435,000 for Diocletian, cited by Treadgold, Byzantium and Its Army 284-1081, isbn:0804731632, ch. 2, not fetched). Convention: comitatenses, limitanei and scholae (all salaried) are counted as active; Gothic and other federates called up under their own leaders are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Gothic federates settled under the 382 treaty, called up under their own leaders (Theodosius led some 20,000 Goths at the Frigidus in 394 according to Jordanes and Orosius, ancient figures), plus other federate and allied bands. Jones (https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, ch. XVII) describes the growing use of federates without a total.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Fleets: John Lydus gives 45,562 men in Diocletian's fleets (as quoted by Jones, https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, p. 679; ancient figure, high). The Notitia fleets (Misenum, Ravenna, river flotillas on the Danube and Rhine) were smaller by 395, and some fleet units are already inside Jones' limitanei totals at 500 men each. Plus ~5,000 staff of the magistri militum and duces.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. The late empire struggled to recruit (conscription levies on landowners, commutation to gold, ever-greater use of barbarian recruits and federates; Jones vol. 2 ch. XVII, https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02). The paper army of ~600,000 was already ~1.2% of the population; 0.025 assumes an emergency levy roughly doubling it.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Legions (comitatenses at ~1,000, old frontier legions at ~3,000 per Jones) and auxilia palatina, plus limitanei infantry (milites, cohortes): ~55-60% of the paper army in Jones' Notitia reconstruction (https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, pp. 681-683) scaled to the active mid; the infantry/cavalry split is not given by Jones and is estimated from his unit-type establishments (cavalry units at 500).

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: mail or scale, ridge helmets, oval shields, spatha, plumbatae; still well equipped from state fabricae but lighter than the Principate legion; frontier units worse equipped.

training.note: Comitatenses professional (0.75), limitanei partly part-time soldier-farmers (0.5); weighted toward the limitanei majority.

count.note: Educated guess. Lanciarii, exculcatores and light auxilia skirmishers; Vegetius describes light-armed troops in every late legion but no total exists.

Educated guess. Sagittarii units in the field armies and frontier commands (several listed in the Notitia) plus archers inside legions (Vegetius says a third to a quarter of recruits trained as archers); no total exists.

Educated guess. Scholae palatinae (3,500 East + 2,500 West per Jones, https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, p. 683), cataphractarii and clibanarii vexillations and heavier equites of the field armies, at Jones' 500 per cavalry unit.

quality.note: Clibanarii in full horse armour on the Persian model, among the era's best (rubric 0.75).

count.note: Educated guess. Equites sagittarii, Dalmatae, Mauri, promoti, scutarii and the many cunei equitum of the limitanei (cavalry units dominate the Notitia lists of the eastern frontier). Total cavalry (heavy + light) ~25-30% of the army is an estimate; Jones gives no cavalry total.

quality.note: Era-typical light horse and horse archers (rubric 0.5-0.75).

training.note: Field-army cavalry professional, frontier cunei lower.

count.note: Educated guess. Vegetius (Epitoma 2.25, written c. 390) gives 55 carroballistae + 10 onagri per legion, but late legions were 1,000-3,000 strong; ballistarii units appear in the Notitia and fortress walls carried mounted engines. Scaled to ~150-200 legion-sized formations and fort garrisons.

quality.note: Torsion artillery still the era's best; onager now standard.

count.note: Educated guess. Liburnians of the Italian and eastern fleets listed in the Notitia (classis Misenatis, Ravennatium, Venetum...); no Mediterranean naval rival existed, so the sea-going fleets were small.

quality.note: Era-typical oared warships, no innovation since the Principate.

count.note: Educated guess. River patrol boats (lusoriae) of the Danube and Rhine flotillas; the Theodosian Code (CTh 7.17.1, AD 412) orders 225 new or rebuilt lusoriae for Moesia and Scythia alone (ancient legal figure, later date).

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: a structured command system (magistri militum, comites, duces, the Notitia hierarchy) and a capable emperor and general (Theodosius, Stilicho), but Adrianople (378) showed poor coordination and the system was riven by usurpations.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.5: regimental identity survived in the field units, but frontier troops were tied to their land, the army had just fought a civil war (Frigidus, 394), and federates served under their own chiefs (rubric 0.25 for those).

morale.note: Rubric 0.5 average: victory at the Frigidus in 394 but the Adrianople disaster (378) still recent, heavy losses on both sides of the civil war, and recruitment by compulsion.

weapons.note: Anchor 3 plus late refinements: spatha, plumbatae, widespread composite bows, onager and arcuballista; short of anchor 4 (no true crossbow or trebuchet in use).

armor.note: Anchor 3 (mail) plus scale and lamellar, ridge helmets and fully armoured clibanarii horse; segmented plate gone, so not above the Trajanic 3.5.

ships.note: Anchor 3: liburnians and river lusoriae; the dromon had not yet appeared.

fortification.note: Anchor 3 exceeded toward anchor 4: late Roman walls with projecting towers, thick curtain walls and city circuits (Aurelian Walls rebuilt), quadriburgia on the frontiers. The Theodosian Land Walls of Constantinople came after 404. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.6 -> 3.45, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for 395 (3.448); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 plus annona militaris in kind, state fabricae, granaries and river transport; network partly degraded in the West.

communications.note: Anchor 3 (mounted relay posts): cursus publicus fully developed.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: exploratores, agentes in rebus, frontier watchtowers.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project Database 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true has no 4th-century values; year 1 CE values for Roman territory (Italy 1,407, Greece 1,275, Egypt 1,116, France 956, Turkey 897, Spain 886) and Egypt 730 CE (1,164) bracket it. The late empire is placed slightly below the 1st-2nd-century average (rome-117: 1,000) for the shrunken western economy; the East was probably at or above its earlier level.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Jones (https://archive.org/details/JonesLaterRomanEmpire02, p. 684) stresses that pay and allowances were issued for ~645,000 men, by far the largest item of the imperial budget (commonly put at half to two-thirds of state spending); with the late Roman tax take at ~6-10% of GDP that implies ~3-7%.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian economy; state fabricae for arms, mints, mines, textiles and construction. Slightly below the Principate.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Egypt and Africa still produced large tax-grain surpluses for Rome and Constantinople and the annona militaris; the West was weaker than in the 2nd century.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: ORBIS v1 (Scheidel & Meeks 2012) models 84,631 km of principal roads and desert tracks (c. 200 CE network, mid); still maintained in 395 apart from Dacia and the Agri Decumates (low), with secondary roads beyond the ORBIS network (high).

majorPorts.note: ORBIS has 268 sea-port sites; ports able to supply a fleet or army (Constantinople, Ostia/Portus, Ravenna, Aquileia, Thessalonica, Alexandria, Carthage, Seleucia Pieria, Ephesus, Corinth, Arelate, Gades...) estimated at ~20.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Grain fleets now served both Rome and Constantinople (the Egyptian annona went east after 330); estimate as for rome-117, lowered for the decline of western trade.

supplyRangeKm.note: By analogy with Engels (isbn:0520042727, ch. 1): pre-modern armies carrying grain and pack animals could operate ~1-2 weeks' march from a depot or navigable water; same as the rome-117 snapshot.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.06-0.11 draft and pack animals per inhabitant x population; cursus publicus and annona transport were large users.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: fortified cities and frontier forts, local supply via the annona; weakened by Gothic federates already inside the empire and limited popular support for a conscript army.

notes: Snapshot = 17 January 395, death of Theodosius I at Milan, the last ruler of the united empire; the empire was divided between Arcadius (East) and Honorius (West, under Stilicho) immediately afterwards. Capital set to Constantinople (Theodosius' main residence); Milan held the western court. Border: historical-basemaps world_400 Western and Eastern Roman Empire polygons (5 years after the snapshot, matching the division of 395). (audit 2026-10-30) Army figures are Notitia Dignitatum reconstructions (Jones 1964); the Notitia lists units, not men, so every total rests on assumed unit establishments, and it is a paper strength. Treadgold (Byzantium and Its Army, ch. 2) and Elton (Warfare in Roman Europe AD 350-425) give similar orders of magnitude but were not fetched. Agathias' 645,000 is an ancient figure shown only as the high bound. The infantry/cavalry split is the weakest part of the force table. Federates are counted as trainedReserves, not active forces.
